What remains justified: both d1p7jd_ and d1ztra1 are classified in homeodomain family a.4.1.1, so they share the family-level evolutionary relationship that SCOPe asserts for that family. Family membership supports a common origin of the homeodomain core and a shared three-helix, helix-turn-helix-type all-alpha architecture, with the same superfamily (a.4.1, homeodomain-like) and class (all-alpha). It also supports the working expectation that both bind DNA through a similar recognition helix. That is a statement about the conserved core fold and broad mechanism, not about every residue or every interaction.

What the shared family does not establish: identical DNA sequence specificity, identical partner or ligand contacts, the same oligomeric state, the same domain boundaries, or the same functional role in a particular organism or complex. Family-level homology supports structural and broad functional inference only. It does not license residue-level transfer of binding-site annotations or specificity.

Why d1ztra1 should not be treated as interchangeable with d1p7jd_: the hf annotation on d1ztra1 marks a feature that the shared family label does not resolve. I cannot reliably state its exact meaning from pretrained knowledge alone. It is an annotation difference that signals d1ztra1 is not a plain drop-in member of the same classification pattern as d1p7jd_, and that difference should be checked against the SCOPe release's annotation definitions before any use. Even without that check, the two entries can differ in loop conformations, DNA or partner contacts, sequence identity, resolution, missing residues, and chain/domain boundaries, all of which matter for template use.

For use as templates: template selection needs a structure-based alignment and residue mapping for the query, not just a shared family code. Choose templates by alignment quality, coverage, resolution, and whether the relevant interface matches the query. Do not assume the two domains are equivalent templates just because they share a.4.1.1.

For use as training examples: treat them as distinct records with their annotations kept as metadata. Group splits by family or superfamily, or by sequence-similarity cluster, so that close homologs do not leak between training and evaluation.
